summary:
Asterion is a free educational game in which players act as NASA engineers. They build real NASA spacecraft from the parts of authentic 3D models, from the MarCO CubeSat to the Curiosity rover, the James Webb Space Telescope and Voyager 1. They pick a launch vehicle and fly 14 missions inspired by real NASA history.

To address Space mission design game, we turned spaceflight engineering into hands-on decisions. Every launch is computed with the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, using stage data for ten launch vehicles such as Saturn V and SLS. Players see thrust-to-weight ratio, Δv margin, orbit and power budget before they launch. Poor design choices lead to realistic failures, followed by a debrief that explains the physics. Players then dock with the ISS and assemble modules in orbit by hand, under a limited budget that rewards efficient engineering.

This matters because most people never see why spacecraft are designed the way they are. Asterion makes those trade-offs playable, so students learn by building, failing and trying again.
details:
Asterion is a game that lets you work as a NASA engineer. Across 14 missions based on real NASA history, from a tiny CubeSat to the Curiosity rover and the James Webb Space Telescope, players build spacecraft from the parts of authentic NASA 3D models, choose a rocket and launch.

Every decision has consequences. Before liftoff, the game runs real calculations: the rocket equation for each stage, thrust-to-weight ratio, Δv margin, orbit and power budget. A flawed design leads to a realistic failure, and a mentor explains the physics behind it. After launch, players fly the mission from mission control, dock with the ISS by hand and assemble modules in orbit, all on a limited budget that rewards smart engineering.

We built it because spaceflight usually feels like distant formulas on a board. Asterion turns those formulas into choices you can see, test and learn from. Our goal is to make students curious about engineering and NASA’s missions.

Tools: Unity 6 (URP), C#, HLSL shaders, glTFast, NASA 3D Resources models, NASA Blue Marble imagery, procedurally generated audio and GitHub.

We balanced scientific accuracy with fun, so that the game runs on ordinary laptops and stays understandable to beginners.
